questions.prompt: What is the result of one relaxing their external intercostal muscles and their diaphragm?
options: Air is forced out of the lungs.
questions.suggestedLabel: A. Air is forced out of the lungs.
questions.suggestedRationale: Relaxing the diaphragm and external intercostals decreases thoracic volume and forces air out (expiration).

questions.prompt: The respiratory mucosa is continuous through the
options: middle ear cavity and auditory tube.
questions.suggestedRationale: Respiratory mucosa is continuous through the upper and lower tracts, sinuses, pharynx, and the auditory tube/middle ear.

questions.prompt: The maximum volume of air a person can exhale after a maximum inspiration is termed the
questions.suggestedLabel: D. vital capacity.
questions.suggestedRationale: Vital capacity is the maximum volume exhaled after a maximum inspiration.

questions.prompt: Which of the following applies to the blood in the pulmonary artery?
options: It is flowing into the left atrium.
questions.suggestedLabel: B. PO2 is low.
questions.suggestedRationale: Pulmonary-artery blood is venous blood going to the lungs, so PO2 is low; hydrostatic pressure there is not high.

questions.prompt: Which of the following causes bronchodilation?
questions.suggestedLabel: A. Epinephrine
questions.suggestedRationale: Epinephrine stimulates β2 receptors and dilates bronchi; histamine, parasympathetic input, and β2 blockers do the opposite.

questions.prompt: The central chemoreceptors in the medulla are normally most sensitive to
questions.suggestedLabel: D. elevated carbon dioxide level.
questions.suggestedRationale: Central chemoreceptors respond primarily to elevated PaCO2 (via CSF pH/H+).

questions.prompt: Oxygen diffuses from the alveoli to the blood because
options: PO2 is higher in the blood.
PO2 is lower in the blood.
CO2 is diffusing out of the blood.
more CO2 is diffusing out of cells into the blood.
questions.suggestedLabel: B. PO2 is lower in the blood.
questions.suggestedRationale: Oxygen diffuses down its pressure gradient because alveolar PO2 is higher than blood PO2.

questions.prompt: Carbon dioxide is primarily transported in the blood
options: attached to the iron molecule in hemoglobin.
questions.suggestedLabel: C. as bicarbonate ion.
questions.suggestedRationale: Most carbon dioxide is carried as bicarbonate ion.

questions.prompt: With respiratory alkalosis (compensated or decompensated) the level of this always decreased:
questions.suggestedLabel: B. PaCO2
questions.suggestedRationale: Respiratory alkalosis is caused by a low PaCO2, so PaCO2 is always decreased; bicarbonate falls only after renal compensation.

questions.prompt: What does carbaminohemoglobin refer to?
options: Replacement of oxygen by carbon monoxide on hemoglobin molecules
Full saturation of all heme molecules by oxygen
Carbon dioxide attached to an amino group on the hemoglobin molecule
Oxygen combined with iron in the hemoglobin molecule
questions.suggestedLabel: C. Carbon dioxide attached to an amino group on the hemoglobin molecule
questions.suggestedRationale: Carbaminohemoglobin is CO2 bound to amino groups on the globin chains, not to heme iron.

questions.prompt: Light bubbly or crackling breathing sounds associated with serous secretions are called
questions.suggestedLabel: C. rales.
questions.suggestedRationale: Light, bubbly crackles from serous secretions are rales (crackles).

questions.prompt: Layrngotracheobronchitis is a ____ and prevalent in ___
options: Viral infection in infant under 12 months
Viral infection in child, 3 months to 3 years
Bacterial infection in infant under 6 months
Bacterial infection in child, 3 to 7 years
questions.suggestedLabel: B. Viral infection in child, 3 months to 3 years
questions.suggestedRationale: Laryngotracheobronchitis (croup) is typically viral and most common in children about 3 months to 3 years old.

questions.prompt: Early signs and symptoms of infectious rhinitis are:
options: Purulent nasal discharge and periorbital pain
Serous nasal discharge, congestion, and sneezing
Copious purulent sputum, particularly in the morning
questions.suggestedLabel: B. Serous nasal discharge, congestion, and sneezing
questions.suggestedRationale: Infectious rhinitis begins with watery discharge, congestion, and sneezing, not purulent drainage.

questions.prompt: Why does the influenza virus cause recurrent infection in individuals?
options: Elderly patients are predisposed to secondary infections.
The virus is transmitted by numerous routes.
The virus is very difficult to destroy.
Viral mutation reduces immunity from prior infections
questions.suggestedLabel: D. Viral mutation reduces immunity from prior infections
questions.suggestedRationale: Antigenic drift or shift means immunity from a prior influenza infection may not protect against a new strain.

questions.prompt: What is the most common cause of viral pneumonia?
questions.suggestedLabel: B. Influenza virus
questions.suggestedRationale: Influenza is the most common cause of viral pneumonia; H. influenzae and pneumococcus are bacteria.

questions.prompt: How does severe hypoxia develop with pneumonia?
options: Oxygen diffusion is impaired by the congestion.
Inflammatory exudate absorbs oxygen from the alveolar air.
Infection reduces effective compensation by the he
questions.suggestedLabel: B. Oxygen diffusion is impaired by the congestion.
questions.suggestedRationale: Alveolar congestion and exudate impair oxygen diffusion and cause hypoxia.

questions.prompt: A Classic sign of Rust color sputum especially in patient population with pneumonia refers to
options: Streptococcus pneumoniae is the infecting agent.
persistent coughing has damaged the mucosa in the bronchi.
questions.suggestedLabel: B. Streptococcus pneumoniae is the infecting agent.
questions.suggestedRationale: Rust-colored sputum is classically associated with Streptococcus pneumoniae (pneumococcal) pneumonia.

questions.prompt: Which of the following are true of Tuberculosis
options: Active secondary infection within tissue occurs when horst resistance is decreased
formation of caseation necrosis with a tuberlce is formed in the lungs
TB is an acid-fast bacillus which is very resistant to many disinfectants and is not limited to just lungs
TB occurs due to HIV and is an opportunistic infection
questions.suggestedLabel: A, B, and C
questions.suggestedRationale: A, B, and C are true of TB (reactivation when resistance falls, caseous tubercles, acid-fast bacillus not limited to the lungs). D overstates the role of HIV; TB is not only an opportunistic HIV infection.

questions.prompt: True or False: Histoplasmosis is a fungal infection
questions.suggestedLabel: A. True
questions.suggestedRationale: Histoplasmosis is a fungal infection.

questions.prompt: Cystic fibrosis is transmitted as a/an
options: X-linked recessive gene and all your glands are involved
autosomal recessive gene and defected exocrine gland
autosomal dominant gene and defected myelin sheath
questions.suggestedLabel: B. autosomal recessive gene and defected exocrine gland
questions.suggestedRationale: Cystic fibrosis is autosomal recessive and affects exocrine glands.

questions.prompt: Growth and development delays of a child with cystic fibrosis is due to?
options: deficit of gastric enzymes for protein digestion.
mucus plugs obstructing the flow of pancreatic enzymes.
lack of available treatment for steatorrhea.
questions.suggestedLabel: B. mucus plugs obstructing the flow of pancreatic enzymes.
questions.suggestedRationale: Thick mucus blocks pancreatic ducts, so digestive enzymes do not reach the intestine and growth is delayed.

questions.prompt: Persistent thick mucus in the bronchioles of a child with cystic fibrosis may cause
questions.suggestedLabel: Air trapping, atelectasis, repeated infections, and irreversible lung damage (1–4)
questions.suggestedRationale: Thick bronchiolar mucus causes air trapping, atelectasis, repeated infections, and irreversible lung damage (1–4). “Black meconium” is not a bronchiole effect, and no listed combo is 1–4 alone.

questions.prompt: Why does hypercalcemia occur with bronchogenic carcinoma?
options: Invasion of the parathyroid gland by the tumor
Secretion of parathyroid or parathyroid like hormones by the tumor ( neoplastic Syndrome)
Failure of the kidney to excrete calcium ions
questions.suggestedLabel: B. Secretion of parathyroid or parathyroid like hormones by the tumor ( neoplastic Syndrome)
questions.suggestedRationale: Hypercalcemia can be a paraneoplastic effect of PTH-like hormone (PTHrP) secretion by some lung tumors.

questions.prompt: Predisposition to aspiration post procedure could be due to?
options: Reduced pressure of the abdominal organs on the diaphragm
Depression of the vomiting center by anesthetics and analgesics
Vomiting caused by drugs or anesthesia
Lack of food intake for the previous 24 hours
questions.suggestedLabel: C. Vomiting caused by drugs or anesthesia
questions.suggestedRationale: Post-procedure aspiration often follows vomiting from drugs or anesthesia while airway-protective reflexes are depressed.

questions.prompt: During an acute asthma attack, how does respiratory obstruction occur?
options: Option 11. Relaxation of bronchial smooth muscle
Increased secretion of thick, tenacious mucus
questions.suggestedRationale: During an acute attack, obstruction comes from mucosal edema and thick mucus (and bronchoconstriction), not from muscle relaxation.

questions.prompt: Barrell chest is a sign of emphysema which is caused due to?
options: Air trapping and hyperinflation with increase in residual lung volume
Dilated bronchi and increased mucous secretions
questions.suggestedLabel: A. Air trapping and hyperinflation with increase in residual lung volume
questions.suggestedRationale: Barrel chest in emphysema reflects air trapping, hyperinflation, and an increased residual volume.

questions.prompt: Which statement or statements apply to emphysema?
options: The surface area available for gas exchange is greatly reduced.
A genetic defect may lead to breakdown of elastic fibers.
questions.suggestedLabel: A, B, and D
questions.suggestedRationale: In emphysema the gas-exchange surface is reduced, elastic-fiber breakdown may be genetic (α1-antitrypsin), and expiration is impaired. V/Q does not stay constant, and no combo option is listed.

questions.prompt: What is the cause of chronic bronchitis?
options: Chronic irritation, inflammation, and recurrent infection of the larger airways
A genetic defect causing excessive production of mucus
Hypersensitivity to parasympathetic stimulation in the bronchi
Deficit of enzymes, preventing tissue degeneration
questions.suggestedLabel: A. Chronic irritation, inflammation, and recurrent infection of the larger airways
questions.suggestedRationale: Chronic bronchitis is chronic irritation, inflammation, and recurrent infection of the larger airways, usually from smoking.

questions.prompt: Why does cor pulmonale develop with chronic pulmonary disease?
options: he right ventricle pumps more blood than the left ventricle.
Pulmonary fibrosis and vasoconstriction increase vascular resistance.
Demands on the left ventricle are excessive.
Blood viscosity is increased, adding to cardiac workload.
questions.suggestedLabel: B. Pulmonary fibrosis and vasoconstriction increase vascular resistance.
questions.suggestedRationale: Pulmonary fibrosis and hypoxic vasoconstriction raise pulmonary vascular resistance and strain the right ventricle (cor pulmonale).

questions.prompt: Restrictive lung disorders can be divided into two groups based on its?
options: patient history of obesity and exposure to other COPD.
previous lung disease and cardiovascular disorders.
anatomical abnormality and lung disease damage, impairing expansion
questions.suggestedLabel: D. anatomical abnormality and lung disease damage, impairing expansion
questions.suggestedRationale: Restrictive disorders are grouped by impaired expansion from chest-wall or anatomic problems, or from lung-tissue damage.

questions.prompt: What is caused by frequent inhalation of irritating particles such as silica?
questions.suggestedLabel: A. Fibrosis and loss of compliance
questions.suggestedRationale: Inhaled silica and similar dusts cause pulmonary fibrosis and loss of compliance (pneumoconiosis).

questions.prompt: Severe Hypoxia is caused by Pulmonary Edema in patients due to?
options: decreased diffusion of carbon dioxide from the alveoli.
interference with expansion of the lungs.
decreased recoil of lungs and ineffective expiration.
questions.suggestedLabel: B. interference with expansion of the lungs.
questions.suggestedRationale: Edema fluid makes the lungs stiffer and interferes with expansion and oxygen transfer, producing severe hypoxia.

questions.prompt: Which of the following is or are a cause of pulmonary edema?
options: Hyperproteinemia and increasing osmotic pressure of the blood
questions.suggestedLabel: A, B, and C
questions.suggestedRationale: Left-sided heart failure, volume overload, and inhaled toxins can cause pulmonary edema. Hyperproteinemia would raise oncotic pressure and does not cause edema; no combo option is listed.

questions.prompt: What is a large-sized pulmonary embolus likely to cause?
questions.suggestedLabel: C. Hypotension and right-sided heart failure
questions.suggestedRationale: A large pulmonary embolus can obstruct outflow, drop systemic pressure, and cause acute right-sided heart failure.

questions.prompt: How does total obstruction of the airway lead to atelectasis?
options: Decreased surfactant production impairs lung expansion.
Air is absorbed from the alveoli distal to the obstruction.
Air continues to be inspired but is trapped distal to the obstruction.
questions.suggestedLabel: C. Air is absorbed from the alveoli distal to the obstruction.
questions.suggestedRationale: Air distal to a complete airway obstruction is absorbed, and those alveoli collapse (absorption atelectasis).

questions.prompt: What is true of Flail Chest? select all that apply
options: An open puncture wound involves the pleural membranes.
Several ribs are fractured at two sites.
The mediastinum shifts toward the unaffected side
Venous return is impaired and cardiac output is reduced
questions.suggestedLabel: B and D
questions.suggestedRationale: Flail chest is several ribs fractured at two sites; paradoxical motion can impair venous return and cardiac output. A describes an open chest wound, and tracheal/mediastinal shift toward the unaffected side is more typical of tension pneumothorax.

questions.prompt: Which of the following is a manifestation of a simple closed pneumothorax?
options: Tracheal deviation toward the unaffected lung
Increased breath sounds on the affected side
questions.suggestedLabel: C. Asymmetrical chest movements
questions.suggestedRationale: A simple closed pneumothorax typically causes uneven chest movement; tracheal deviation away from the lesion suggests tension pneumothorax.

questions.prompt: Which of the following is an effect of a large open pneumothorax (sucking wound)?
questions.suggestedLabel: A. Mediastinal flutter, impairing venous return
questions.suggestedRationale: A large open (“sucking”) pneumothorax lets the mediastinum flutter and impairs venous return.

questions.prompt: What is true of Adult Respiratory Distress Syndrome
options: Damage leading to increased permeability of the alveolar capillary membranes
Decreased surface tension in the alveoli
Excessive fluid and protein interstitially and in the alveoli
Multiple diffuse hemorrhages in the lungs
questions.suggestedRationale: ARDS is alveolar-capillary injury with protein-rich fluid in the interstitium and alveoli; surfactant loss raises (does not lower) surface tension.

questions.prompt: Laryngotracheobronchitis manifestation sign is typically:
options: sore and scratchy throat with fever.
questions.suggestedLabel: B. hoarse voice and barking cough.
questions.suggestedRationale: Croup classically presents with a hoarse voice and a barking cough.

questions.prompt: SARS presents with a flulike syndrome followed, after a few days, by
options: increased exudates in the bronchial tree and pleural cavity.
interstitial lung congestion, dyspnea, and dry cough.
hemoptysis and necrosis of mucous membrane.
questions.suggestedLabel: C. interstitial lung congestion, dyspnea, and dry cough.
questions.suggestedRationale: After a flulike prodrome, SARS typically progresses to interstitial congestion, dyspnea, and a dry cough.

questions.prompt: Significant early sign of bronchogenic carcinoma in a smoker is
options: Production of large volumes of purulent sputum
questions.suggestedLabel: A. Frequent nonproductive cough
questions.suggestedRationale: A persistent, often nonproductive cough in a smoker is an important early warning; hemoptysis and weight loss tend to appear later.

questions.prompt: Which of the following drugs in an inhaler would likely be carried by individuals to provide immediate control of acute asthma attacks?
questions.suggestedLabel: D. A b2-adrenergic agent
questions.suggestedRationale: A short-acting β2-agonist inhaler is used for immediate relief of an acute asthma attack.

questions.prompt: Primary atypical pneumonia (PAP) is caused by
questions.suggestedLabel: C. Mycoplasma pneumoniae.
questions.suggestedRationale: Primary atypical (walking) pneumonia is classically caused by Mycoplasma pneumoniae.

questions.prompt: Which factor usually causes metabolic acidosis to develop in association with hypoxia?
questions.suggestedLabel: A. Anaerobic metabolism
questions.suggestedRationale: Severe hypoxia drives anaerobic metabolism and lactic (metabolic) acidosis.

questions.prompt: Cytokine storm particularly in patients 60 and older is a unique pathophysiological characteristic of
questions.suggestedLabel: C. Covid-19.
questions.suggestedRationale: A cytokine storm is a distinctive, severe feature of COVID-19, especially in older adults.

questions.prompt: Virchow’s triad refers to
options: an anatomical structure in the kidneys.
a combination of factors affecting potential thrombus formation.
factors that predispose an individual toward urinary tract infections.
psychological factors leading to stress associated with immobility
questions.suggestedLabel: B. a combination of factors affecting potential thrombus formation.
questions.suggestedRationale: Virchow’s triad is the combination of factors that promote thrombus formation (stasis, vessel injury, and hypercoagulability).

questions.prompt: Lack of weight-bearing and skeletal muscle activity for a prolonged period leads to
options: bone demineralization and decreased skeletal muscle mass.
questions.suggestedLabel: D. bone demineralization and decreased skeletal muscle mass.
questions.suggestedRationale: Prolonged lack of weight-bearing leads to both bone demineralization and decreased skeletal muscle mass.

questions.prompt: The major problem associated with immobility and the gastrointestinal tract is
questions.suggestedLabel: A. constipation.
questions.suggestedRationale: Reduced gastrointestinal motility from immobility commonly leads to constipation.

questions.prompt: Prolonged immobility may predispose to ___________ in the kidneys.
questions.suggestedLabel: D. all of these
questions.suggestedRationale: Immobility predisposes to urinary stasis, renal calculi, and infection.

questions.prompt: Immobility may lead to dehydration primarily as a result of
options: changes in hormonal secretions due to increased blood in the thorax.
destruction of the kidneys as a result of ischemia and necrosis.
blockage of the ureters, causing retention of urine.
toxins being produced by infectious microorganisms.
questions.suggestedLabel: A. changes in hormonal secretions due to increased blood in the thorax.
questions.suggestedRationale: Recumbency shifts blood into the thorax and changes hormone release (including natriuretic peptide), increasing fluid loss and contributing to dehydration.
